Bipartite Network Analysis

Cassy Dorff, Shahryar Minhas, and Tosin Salau

2026-11-22

Source: vignettes/articles/bipartite.Rmd
bipartite.Rmd
library(lame)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(6886)

Introduction

Many real-world networks are bipartite: two distinct types of nodes, with ties forming only between types, never within them. Students enroll in courses, countries sign treaties, legislators join committees. The adjacency matrix is rectangular rather than square, and the row and column nodes play fundamentally different roles.

Both ame() (cross-sectional) and lame() (longitudinal) support bipartite networks. The key difference from the unipartite case is that the model uses separate latent spaces for the two node types, connected by an interaction matrix GG.

The Bipartite AME Model

In a bipartite network, the probability of a tie between row node ii and column node jj is modeled as:

yij=β′xij+ai+bj+ui′Gvj+ϵijy_{ij} = \beta'x_{ij} + a_i + b_j + u_i'Gv_j + \epsilon_{ij}

The additive effects work as in the unipartite case (see the cross-sectional vignette): aia_i captures how “active” row node ii is, bjb_j how “popular” column node jj is. The multiplicative term ui′Gvju_i'Gv_j replaces the unipartite ui′vju_i'v_j: row and column nodes live in potentially different-dimensional latent spaces (RrowR_\text{row} and RcolR_\text{col}), and GG is a Rrow×RcolR_\text{row} \times R_\text{col} interaction matrix.

How GG enters differs between the cross-sectional and longitudinal entry points:

  • In ame() (cross-sectional bipartite), GG is a rank-truncated scaled identity, held fixed during MCMC. The rotation and scaling of the interaction are carried by UU and VV, and the identified quantity is the overall multiplicative term UGV′U G V'.
  • In lame() (longitudinal bipartite), the sampler draws GG each iteration from its conditional Gaussian, and one GG is shared across periods (see Time-varying interaction matrix below).

In either case, the row-side positions (UU, shape nrow×Rrown_\text{row} \times R_\text{row}) and column-side positions (VV, shape ncol×Rcoln_\text{col} \times R_\text{col}) can be chosen at different ranks.

Two terms are absent in the bipartite setting: the dyadic correlation ρ\rho (a row actor is never also a column actor, so there is no reciprocal tie to correlate), and the joint covariance of aa and bb, which instead have independent variances since they describe different types of actors.

Supported families in bipartite mode

Every family that fits a square network also fits a rectangular one, in both ame() and lame(). Each cell is independent given the linear predictor, because a bipartite graph has no reciprocal cell.

Family Tie type
normal continuous values.
binary tie / no tie, probit link.
ordinal ordered categories, with cutpoints induced by the data.
cbin censored binary, with odmax as the per-row cap on ties.
frn fixed rank nominations; each row’s top odmax ranks are observed.
poisson counts; period_exposure supplies a per-period offset in lame().

Cross-Sectional Analysis with ame()

Coming from long-format data?

If your data lives in a long-format table (patient_id, drug, prescribed), build a bipartite netify object and pass it directly to ame():

rx_net <- netify::netify(
    rx,
    actor1 = "patient_id",
    actor2 = "drug",
    weight = "prescribed",
    mode = "bipartite",
    symmetric = FALSE,
    missing_to_zero = FALSE
)

fit <- ame(rx_net, family = "binary", mode = "bipartite", R = 2)

Row and column names carry through to fit$APM (one number per patient) and fit$BPM (one number per drug) downstream. Use missing_to_zero = TRUE only when absent patient-drug rows are observed non-prescriptions rather than unobserved dyads.

Simulating Data

We simulate a bipartite network of 30 students and 20 courses, each with a 2-dimensional latent position; the interaction matrix GG determines how those dimensions combine to predict enrollment.

# simulate a student-course enrollment network
n_students <- 30
n_courses <- 20

# true latent positions (unobserved in practice)
U_true <- matrix(rnorm(n_students * 2, 0, 0.8), n_students, 2)
V_true <- matrix(rnorm(n_courses * 2, 0, 0.8), n_courses, 2)

# interaction matrix: positive affinity on dimension 1, negative on dimension 2
G_true <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, -1), 2, 2)

# enrollment ties; the negative intercept keeps enrollment near 25-30%
eta <- -0.8 + U_true %*% G_true %*% t(V_true)
prob <- pnorm(eta)
Y_bipartite <- matrix(
    rbinom(n_students * n_courses, 1, prob),
    n_students,
    n_courses
)

rownames(Y_bipartite) <- paste0("Student", 1:n_students)
colnames(Y_bipartite) <- paste0("Course", 1:n_courses)

cat("Network dimensions:", dim(Y_bipartite), "\n")
#> Network dimensions: 30 20
cat("Enrollment rate:", round(mean(Y_bipartite), 2), "\n")
#> Enrollment rate: 0.29

Fitting the Model

Fitting a bipartite model requires setting mode = "bipartite" and specifying the latent dimensions for each node type separately via R_row and R_col.

# two chains by default; summary() ends with the between-chain check
fit_cross <- ame(
    Y = Y_bipartite,
    mode = "bipartite",
    R_row = 2, # latent dimensions for students
    R_col = 2, # latent dimensions for courses
    family = "binary",
    burn = 500,
    nscan = 2000,
    odens = 5,
    verbose = FALSE,
    # save thinned U/V draws so latent_positions() reports posterior SDs
    posterior_opts = posterior_options(save_UV = TRUE)
)

summary(fit_cross)
#> 
#> ── AME model summary ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Call 
#> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + U[i,1:2] %*% G %*% V[j,1:2]', family = 'binary'
#> 
#> ── Regression coefficients 
#>           Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat Threshold
#> intercept   -0.793    0.113  -7.022       0   -1.011   -0.578 1.006      1.05
#>               ESS    
#> intercept 462.819 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use
#>   the credible intervals.
#> 
#> ── Variance components 
#>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold      ESS
#> va    0.050    0.022 1.001      1.05  864.628
#> vb    0.059    0.029 1.000      1.05 1022.309
#>   va = row variance, vb = column variance
#> • Latent dimensions: 96%, 4% of the latent product
#> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity
#>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws
#>   reach by chance, if larger.
#> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

The summary shows the intercept (we included no covariates) and the variance components. The fitted object also stores student latent positions (U), course latent positions (V), the (fixed) interaction matrix (G), and additive effects (APM for student activity, BPM for course popularity).

Visualizing the Latent Space

uv_plot with layout = "biplot" places both node types in the same latent space: students and courses that appear close together have a higher predicted probability of a tie.

uv_plot(fit_cross, layout = "biplot") +
    ggtitle("Bipartite latent space: students and courses")

In ame() the estimated quantity is the overall multiplicative term UGV′U G V', and fit_cross$U and fit_cross$V are its factors: they factor the posterior mean of that product, so they are posterior summaries, not a single draw. layout = "heatmap" draws the product itself, students against courses, with each side ordered by clustering:

uv_plot(fit_cross, layout = "heatmap")

With nodes = "col" the heatmap shows how similar the courses are: the cosine between their columns of the product, using every fitted dimension. Courses with similarity near 1 draw the same students, near -1 opposite ones. Courses in grey have positions not distinguishable from zero, so they have no direction to compare; they are placed last and named in the caption. latent_similarity(fit_cross, "col") returns the same matrix. Because the latent product is centred, similarity is measured against the average course: courses with no pattern of their own sit opposite that average and look similar to each other.

uv_plot(fit_cross, layout = "heatmap", nodes = "col")

Longitudinal Analysis with lame()

When bipartite networks are observed over multiple time periods (enrollments across semesters, country–treaty memberships across decades), lame() pools information across time while optionally allowing the latent structure to evolve.

Simulating Longitudinal Data

We simulate a panel of user–item networks over 5 periods whose latent positions drift via an AR(1) process with ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9. We use the normal family for a continuous outcome; the same calls fit the other families. The data-generating GG is constant across periods, which is what lame() estimates. The chunk writes the AR(1) in its stationary-variance form (Ut=ρUt−1+1−ρ2ϵU_t = \rho\,U_{t-1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,\epsilon with ϵ∼N(0,I)\epsilon \sim N(0, I), marginal variance held at 1), and the sampler reports the innovation-variance form (Ut=ρUt−1+ϵU_t = \rho\,U_{t-1} + \epsilon with ϵ∼N(0,σuv2)\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)); the two coincide when σuv2=1−ρ2\sigma_{uv}^2 = 1 - \rho^2.

n_periods <- 5
n_users <- 20
n_items <- 15

true_rho <- 0.9
G_long <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.3, -0.8), 2, 2)

U_t <- vector("list", n_periods)
V_t <- vector("list", n_periods)
U_t[[1]] <- matrix(rnorm(n_users * 2), n_users, 2)
V_t[[1]] <- matrix(rnorm(n_items * 2), n_items, 2)
for (t in 2:n_periods) {
    U_t[[t]] <- true_rho * U_t[[t - 1]] +
        sqrt(1 - true_rho^2) * matrix(rnorm(n_users * 2), n_users, 2)
    V_t[[t]] <- true_rho * V_t[[t - 1]] +
        sqrt(1 - true_rho^2) * matrix(rnorm(n_items * 2), n_items, 2)
}

Y_list <- list()
for (t in 1:n_periods) {
    eta_t <- U_t[[t]] %*% G_long %*% t(V_t[[t]])
    # continuous outcome: the latent term plus Gaussian noise
    Y_list[[t]] <- eta_t +
        matrix(rnorm(n_users * n_items, 0, 0.5), n_users, n_items)
    rownames(Y_list[[t]]) <- paste0("User", 1:n_users)
    colnames(Y_list[[t]]) <- paste0("Item", 1:n_items)
}
names(Y_list) <- paste0("T", 1:n_periods)

cat("Time periods:", length(Y_list), "\n")
#> Time periods: 5
cat("Dimensions per period:", dim(Y_list[[1]]), "\n")
#> Dimensions per period: 20 15
cat("Average edge weight:", round(mean(sapply(Y_list, mean)), 2), "\n")
#> Average edge weight: -0.01
cat("True latent AR(1) coefficient:", true_rho, "\n")
#> True latent AR(1) coefficient: 0.9

Static Model

The simplest longitudinal model holds latent positions and additive effects constant over time, pooling all periods into a single, more precise estimate per actor.

fit_static <- lame(
    Y = Y_list,
    mode = "bipartite",
    R_row = 2,
    R_col = 2,
    family = "normal",
    dynamic_uv = FALSE,
    dynamic_ab = FALSE,
    burn = 500,
    nscan = 2000,
    odens = 20,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

summary(fit_static)
#> 
#> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Call 
#> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + U[i,1:2] %*% G %*% V[j,1:2]', family = 'normal'

#> • Time periods: 5
#> • Family: normal
#> • Mode: bipartite
#> • Latent dimensions: 91%, 9% of the latent product
#> ℹ Static fit: U, V, a and b are shared across the 5 periods, and per-period
#> predictions vary through the per-period covariates. `dynamic_uv = TRUE` and
#> `dynamic_ab = TRUE` let them vary over time.
#> 
#> ── Regression coefficients 
#>           Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat Threshold
#> intercept   -0.011    0.024  -0.457   0.648   -0.056    0.038 1.008      1.05
#>           ESS  
#> intercept 400  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use
#>   the credible intervals.
#> 
#> ── Variance components 
#>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold ESS
#> va    0.020    0.007 1.001      1.05 400
#> vb    0.021    0.008 1.001      1.05 400
#> ve    0.905    0.034 0.997      1.05 400
#>   va = row variance, vb = column variance, ve = residual variance
#> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity
#>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws
#>   reach by chance, if larger.
#> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

Dynamic Model

When the latent structure changes over time (tastes shift, items gain or lose popularity), the dynamic model lets latent positions and additive effects drift via AR(1) processes: ρ\rho close to 1 means slow, gradual change; close to 0, near-independent structure from period to period.

# same run length as the static fit
fit_dynamic <- lame(
    Y = Y_list,
    mode = "bipartite",
    R_row = 2,
    R_col = 2,
    family = "normal",
    dynamic_uv = TRUE,
    dynamic_ab = TRUE,
    burn = 500,
    nscan = 2000,
    odens = 20,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

summary(fit_dynamic)
#> 
#> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Call 
#> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + U[i,1:2] %*% G %*% V[j,1:2]', family = 'normal'
#> 
#> ── Model 
#> • Time periods: 5
#> • Family: normal
#> • Mode: bipartite
#> • Dynamic latent positions: enabled (kind = ar1, rho_uv = 0.906)
#> • Dynamic additive effects: enabled (rho_ab = 0.583)
#>   rho_ab: posterior sd 0.105 is 0.83 of the prior sd 0.126: the data barely
#>   inform it.
#> • Dynamic regression coefficients: enabled (kind = rw1)
#> 
#> ── Regression coefficients 
#>           Estimate StdError z_value p_value CI_lower CI_upper  Rhat Threshold
#> intercept    0.009    0.018    <NA>    <NA>   -0.026     0.05 1.014      1.05

#> intercept <NA>  
#> ---

#> ℹ Stars are a visual hint from the posterior mean / SD only; for inference use
#>   the credible intervals.
#> ℹ intercept is a coefficient path: the row gives the mean level over the
#>   periods and its interval, with no z or p-value. The periods are below.
#> 
#> ── Dynamic coefficients per period 
#>            Mean    Min   Max Drift Drift_pct Dynamic
#> intercept 0.009 -0.034 0.049 0.082   931.231       Y
#> 
#> ── intercept by period 
#>    Estimate StdError CI_lower CI_upper
#> T1    0.044    0.032   -0.025    0.102
#> T2   -0.013    0.032   -0.081    0.041
#> T3   -0.034    0.032   -0.099    0.032
#> T4    0.049    0.037   -0.025    0.122
#> T5   -0.001    0.037   -0.072    0.079
#> 
#> ── Variance components 
#>    Estimate StdError  Rhat Threshold     ESS
#> va    0.017    0.006 1.010      1.05 281.075
#> vb    0.019    0.007 0.998      1.05 330.000
#> ve    0.249    0.010 0.999      1.05 330.000
#>   va = row variance, vb = column variance, ve = residual variance
#>   Under `dynamic_ab`, va and vb are the variances of the actor levels; rho_ab
#>   and sigma_ab describe the per-period deviations around them.
#> ℹ Threshold is the R-hat the between-chain gate held each monitored quantity
#>   to: 1.05, or the R-hat that settled chains with the same effective draws
#>   reach by chance, if larger.
#> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

The dynamic model reports estimated AR(1) persistence parameters for the latent positions (rho_uv) and additive effects (rho_ab).

cat(sprintf(
    "True rho_uv = %.2f | posterior mean = %.3f | 95%% CI = [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
    true_rho,
    mean(fit_dynamic$rho_uv),
    quantile(fit_dynamic$rho_uv, 0.025),
    quantile(fit_dynamic$rho_uv, 0.975)
))
#> True rho_uv = 0.90 | posterior mean = 0.906 | 95% CI = [0.870, 0.934]

rho_uv is the persistence of the latent positions. The data inform it through the products UtGVt′U_t G V_t', so read it alongside the innovation scale, and use the per-period products in fit_dynamic$UVPM to study how the fitted structure changes: they do not depend on the orientation of the coordinates.

rho_ab is the persistence of the per-period deviations of the sender and receiver effects around each actor’s level. The levels are pooled over time, and va and vb in the summary are their variances. The simulated outcome is UtGVt′U_t G V_t' plus noise, with no sender or receiver activity, and the fit reports that: va and vb are 0.017 and 0.019, against a residual variance of 0.249. The summary line under rho_ab compares its posterior sd with its prior sd, which shows how much the data say about it. On data with period-to-period swings in activity, read rho_ab as you read rho_uv, alongside its own variance component.

Time-varying interaction matrix

lame() estimates one interaction matrix GG for the whole panel, and the positions carry change over time. With time-varying positions, UtGtVt′=(UtGt)Vt′U_t G_t V_t' = (U_t G_t) V_t': movement in GtG_t and movement in the positions give the same likelihood, so the model places its temporal prior on the positions and estimates one GG.

To study how the interaction between the two latent spaces changes over time, fit dynamic_uv = TRUE and read the per-period product fit$UVPM, an nrow×ncol×Tn_\text{row} \times n_\text{col} \times T array, which is the quantity the likelihood identifies.

Visualizing Temporal Evolution

With dynamic effects, uv_plot can show trajectories: each line traces one actor’s latent position from the first to the last period. With 35 actors a per-actor legend and labels would swamp the panel, so we suppress both and read the plot for the overall pattern: positions drift gradually and stay clustered rather than scattering.

uv_plot(fit_dynamic, plot_type = "trajectory", label.nodes = FALSE) +
    guides(color = "none") +
    ggtitle("Dynamic latent trajectories")

To inspect specific actors, pass their names to highlight =: the named actors are coloured (and identified in the legend) while every other trajectory is greyed out.

uv_plot(
    fit_dynamic,
    plot_type = "trajectory",
    highlight = c("User1", "User5", "Item3"),
    label.nodes = FALSE
) +
    ggtitle("Highlighted actor trajectories")

Convergence Diagnostics

trace_plot() shows the draws of the dynamic fit, coloured by chain. The dyadic correlation and sender-receiver covariance are structural constants in bipartite mode (fixed at zero; for a binary bipartite fit the probit error variance is likewise fixed at 1), so we exclude them and the panels show only sampled parameters.

trace_plot(
    fit_dynamic,
    exclude = c("Dyadic correlation", "Sender-receiver covariance")
)

Look for traces that mix well (no long flat stretches or slow drifts) and densities that are smooth and unimodal. The numerical check is the between-chain R̂\hat R verdict that closes each summary() above, and all three fits in this article pass it; fit_dynamic$rhat holds the per-parameter values. For further diagnostics – posterior::summarise_draws() for split-R̂\hat R and ESS, ame(..., chains = 4) for a comparison across more chains, prior_summary(), and loo::loo() after refitting with save_log_lik = TRUE – see the worked end-to-end stack in the cross-sectional vignette.

Comparing Static and Dynamic Models

Is the dynamic model worth the added complexity? The goodness-of-fit plots provide one comparison: if the dynamic model’s posterior-predictive distributions better cover the observed statistics, the extra flexibility is paying off. In each panel the observed statistic at each period is a solid black line with filled points, the posterior-predictive median a dashed grey line, and the grey band the 95% posterior-predictive credible interval. The Gaussian bipartite checks are sender heterogeneity, receiver heterogeneity and weighted four-cycle dependence (the average product of centered, standardized values around fully observed rectangles). Compare all three for each fitted period.

# GOF panels for the static and dynamic fits
gof_plot(fit_static)

gof_plot(fit_dynamic)

The following boxplots summarize the two degree statistics across periods: the SD of row means (how much users vary in activity) and the SD of column means (how much items vary in popularity).

gof_static <- fit_static$GOF
gof_dynamic <- fit_dynamic$GOF

# time-averaged posterior predictive draws (column 1 is the observed value)
extract_ppc <- function(gof, stat) {
    mat <- gof[[stat]]
    colMeans(mat[, -1, drop = FALSE])
}

# observed values averaged over periods
obs_vals <- c(
    mean(gof_static$sd.rowmean[, 1]),
    mean(gof_static$sd.colmean[, 1])
)

# each model contributes its own number of saved draws
ppc_df <- function(gof, model) {
    n <- ncol(gof$sd.rowmean) - 1
    data.frame(
        value = c(extract_ppc(gof, "sd.rowmean"), extract_ppc(gof, "sd.colmean")),
        model = model,
        statistic = rep(c("Row mean SD", "Column mean SD"), each = n)
    )
}
gof_df <- rbind(ppc_df(gof_static, "Static"), ppc_df(gof_dynamic, "Dynamic"))

obs_df <- data.frame(
    statistic = c("Row mean SD", "Column mean SD"),
    observed = obs_vals
)

# posterior-predictive medians quoted in the text below
ppc_med <- with(gof_df, tapply(value, list(model, statistic), median))
ve_static <- round(mean(fit_static$VC[, "ve"]), 3)
ve_dynamic <- round(mean(fit_dynamic$VC[, "ve"]), 3)

ggplot(gof_df, aes(x = model, y = value)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_hline(
        data = obs_df,
        aes(yintercept = observed),
        linetype = 2
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~statistic, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(
        title = "GOF comparison: static vs dynamic",
        subtitle = "Dashed line = observed value",
        x = "Model", y = "Simulated statistic"
    ) +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        panel.border = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = "black"),
        strip.text = element_text(color = "white", hjust = 0)
    )

The dynamic model fits these data better, and the clearest evidence is per period. The residual variance ve falls from 0.905 in the static fit to 0.249 in the dynamic fit, against the 0.25 noise variance we simulated (noise sd 0.5). In gof_plot(fit_dynamic) the posterior-predictive median follows the observed sender heterogeneity as it moves from period to period (0.35, 0.49, 0.18, 0.36, 0.37), while in gof_plot(fit_static) the median is essentially flat. The boxplot averages each statistic across the five periods within each draw (colMeans), so it shows the time-averaged part of that difference: the posterior-predictive medians, dynamic versus static, are 0.37 versus 0.38 against an observed 0.35 for the row-mean SD, and 0.17 versus 0.23 against 0.14 for the column-mean SD. To judge whether a dynamic fit earns its complexity, read the time-averaged boxplot together with ve, the per-period gof_plot(), and loo::loo_compare().

Choosing Latent Dimensions

The latent dimensions (R_row, R_col) control how rich the multiplicative structure is; a practical way to choose them is to fit at several ranks and compare GOF statistics.

# R = 0 is the no-latent-space baseline
dims_to_test <- list(
    c(0, 0),
    c(1, 1),
    c(2, 2)
)

# observed GOF statistics
obs_gof <- gof_stats(Y_bipartite, mode = "bipartite")

gof_results <- list()
for (i in seq_along(dims_to_test)) {
    fit_temp <- ame(
        Y = Y_bipartite,
        mode = "bipartite",
        R_row = dims_to_test[[i]][1],
        R_col = dims_to_test[[i]][2],
        family = "binary",
        burn = 200,
        nscan = 2500,
        odens = 5,
        verbose = FALSE
    )
    # one-sided posterior predictive tail probabilities
    gof_results[[i]] <- c(
        R_row = dims_to_test[[i]][1],
        R_col = dims_to_test[[i]][2],
        pval_rowmean = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "sd.rowmean"] >= obs_gof["sd.rowmean"]),
        pval_colmean = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "sd.colmean"] >= obs_gof["sd.colmean"]),
        pval_fourcycles = mean(fit_temp$GOF[, "four.cycles"] >= obs_gof["four.cycles"])
    )
}

do.call(rbind, gof_results)

These are one-sided posterior predictive tail probabilities, not formal test p-values: values near 0.5 mean the observed statistic lies in the bulk of the predictive distribution, while values near 0 or 1 flag systematic over- or under-prediction. For ame(), fit$GOF stores the observed statistic in row 1, so the calculation includes that one point. The relationship to R is not monotonic, so choose the smallest rank at which the important statistics fall away from the endpoints. If degree statistics remain at an endpoint across ranks while four-cycle statistics are well reproduced, adding dimensions is not addressing the source of the mismatch.

Practical Guidance

When to use bipartite models. Use bipartite mode whenever ties only form between two fundamentally different types of nodes. A rectangular adjacency matrix almost certainly needs it, and even a square one (say, 20 students and 20 courses) does when rows and columns represent different kinds of entities.

Interpreting the output. The additive effects (APM, BPM) are the most directly interpretable: which row nodes are unusually active and which column nodes unusually popular, after controlling for covariates and latent structure. The latent positions (U, V) and interaction matrix (G) capture residual association, answering “beyond the covariates and overall activity levels, which row nodes tend to connect to which column nodes?”

Extracting Positions for Custom Analysis

If you need the latent positions in a tidy format, latent_positions() returns a data frame with one row per actor-dimension-time combination. The posterior_sd column is populated here because fit_cross stored thinned U/V draws via posterior_opts = posterior_options(save_UV = TRUE); without that option the column is NA and a refit hint is printed.

lp <- latent_positions(fit_cross)
head(lp)
#>      actor dimension time       value posterior_sd type
#> 1 Student1         1    1  0.92664928    0.4070340    U
#> 2 Student2         1    1 -0.06600046    0.3098522    U
#> 3 Student3         1    1 -1.32145387    0.4524009    U
#> 4 Student4         1    1  1.69250957    0.5217933    U
#> 5 Student5         1    1 -0.60815235    0.3155654    U
#> 6 Student6         1    1 -1.56906407    0.4978761    U

# row nodes (students) only
lp_students <- lp[lp$type == "U", ]
cat("Student positions:", nrow(lp_students), "rows\n")
#> Student positions: 60 rows

This is especially useful for bipartite networks where U (row nodes) and V (column nodes) have different numbers of actors.
